title: Calm first, or insight first?
hookLine: a tray of blue flowers, packed so tight no stalk shows, and an old argument about what comes first
carry: calm or insight first: the path opens both ways
tomorrow: what happens if you just look at yellow, and nothing else?

lines: CLEAN DESK FIRST, OR START IN THE MESS?
A TRAY OF BLUE FLOWERS. BLUE, BLUE.
cards: Some people can't start homework until the desk is clear, the tabs are closed and the tea is made. Others start in the middle of the mess and tidy as they go.

Both get it done, and each thinks the other way is a little strange. Meditators have their own version of that argument, and it's yesterday's question: do you need deep calm before you can see clearly?

Today's disc sits right in the middle of it. Buddhaghosa says to fill a tray with blue flowers, packed so tight that no stalk or gap shows. Or stretch blue cloth across a frame like the skin of a drum.
Then look, and say quietly: blue, blue.

teach.b: The first view says: start here. A disc like this builds calm, and the manual gives whole chapters to discs like it. Its best case: a shaking lamp can't light a page.
Settle the mind on one color until it's steady and bright, then turn it toward how things are. Insight from a steady mind goes deeper and holds. The second view says: start with insight.
The commentaries have a name for a meditator who does: dry insight, going straight to watching body and mind rise and pass, with the calm that close watching brings.
Its best case: discs take time, quiet and a teacher, and plenty of people have none of those.

teach.h: INSIGHT FIRST: CHANGE IS HERE NOW.
teach.b: Change is right here in any life, today, and looking at it closely is how the path begins. Now the twist. Both sides quote the same short sutta.
In it, Ananda, the Buddha's companion, says some develop calm and then insight.
Some develop insight and then calm. Some yoke the two together, like a pair of oxen.
And for each of them, he says, the path can open. Teachers still argue about which order to recommend. The text leaves the gate wide.

how: Theravada teachers differ on the order of practice: some train deep calm with a kasina such as the blue disc before turning to insight, while others teach insight from the start; both point to the Buddha's teaching on calm and insight.

o: the low, sad mood that meditation is meant to cure
the robe color monks wear to show they've left home
a disc of pure color gazed at until the mind steadies

games.q: who says what about the order — tap the pairs.
p: a steady lamp lights the page
change is here to watch today

s: Buddhist meditation has one fixed order everyone follows
Ananda names calm then insight, insight then calm, and both yoked together.
the blue disc can be made of flowers, or of cloth stretched like a drum
either way, nothing but the color should show.
both sides of the debate quote the same sutta
Ananda's short teaching leaves room for each order.

games.q: someone at your meditation group says you must master calm with a disc before any insight practice. state the other side's best case.
o: insight is the advanced stuff, so skipping ahead is just smarter.
calm practice is old-fashioned, and nobody needs it anymore.
the commentaries name dry insight: watching change can begin today.
games.why: that's the strongest version: named in the tradition's own commentaries, and Ananda allows insight first. the calm side's best case is just as real: a steady mind sees further.

practice: Find something blue near you: a shirt, a mug, a patch of sky. Let your eyes rest on the color itself, not the object or what it's for. When a thought pulls you off, say blue, blue, and come back.

wordCard.voice: Blue: nila in Pali. A disc of pure color, and a doorway into an old argument about what comes first.

orig.note: Pali: blue, dark blue. The color disc held in mind with the plain word, blue, blue.

carryVoice: Your line: calm first or insight first, and Ananda says the path can open either way. Blue sits in front of both. That's day ten of forty.

sources.ref: Visuddhimagga 5 (the blue kasina: blue flowers filling a tray or basket so no stamens or stalks show, or blue cloth stretched like a drum face, or blue metal or paint; noted as 'blue, blue')
Anguttara Nikaya 4.170 (Yuganaddha Sutta: Ananda on calm preceded by insight, insight preceded by calm, and the two yoked together, each leading to the arising of the path)
Pali commentaries (the sukkhavipassaka, 'dry-insight' meditator who develops insight without first attaining jhana)
